7100:
Good-natured describes a person who has a naturally kind, cheerful, and pleasant disposition. It means they are consistently friendly, easy to get along with, and not easily upset, angered, or irritated — and crucially, this isn't something they have to try hard at. It comes from within. It is simply who they are.

The word is built on the idea of one's nature — your natural inner personality and temperament. A good-natured person's default setting is warmth, patience, and pleasantness.

Think of the most easygoing, warm person you know — the one who always seems relaxed and cheerful, who makes everyone feel comfortable, who laughs things off rather than brooding, who rarely snaps or complains even when things go wrong. That person is almost certainly good-natured.

In everyday life, a good-natured person stays calm and pleasant even in mildly frustrating situations. When someone teases or jokes with them, they laugh along instead of taking offense. When others make mistakes, they respond with patience rather than criticism. They don't hold grudges. They don't have a short fuse. Being around them just feels easy.
It Describes a Consistent Trait, Not a Moment

This is an important nuance. Good-natured refers to a person's overall temperament — something stable and reliable about who they are, not a one-time act of kindness or a good mood on a particular day. You wouldn't call someone good-natured just because they smiled at you once. It means they are reliably and consistently warm, pleasant, and cheerful across situations and over time.
It Can Describe More Than Just People

While most commonly used for people, good-natured can also describe behaviors, remarks, laughter, or interactions:

"Good-natured teasing" means playful, friendly joking that isn't meant to hurt anyone. "Good-natured laughter" is warm laughter that includes everyone rather than mocking someone. "A good-natured debate" is one where both sides stay friendly and light, without hostility.

In all these cases, the word signals that something was done in a warm, friendly, non-hostile spirit.

Good-natured does not mean weak or a pushover. A good-natured person can absolutely stand their ground and express disagreement — they just do so without being harsh, cold, or hostile.

It does not mean fake niceness. Someone who performs pleasantness for social reasons but secretly resents everything is not good-natured. True good-naturedness is genuine — it comes from within, not from strategy.

It also does not mean naive or gullible. Being cheerful and warm has nothing to do with being easily fooled.

• "Even after the long delay, she remained good-natured and kept the conversation light."
  • "He's so good-natured that even when people tease him, he just laughs along."
  • "The teacher's good-natured humor made the class feel relaxed and enjoyable."
  • "It was just good-natured banter between old friends — nobody meant any harm."
  • "What I admire most about him is his good-natured patience; nothing seems to rattle him for long."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Amiable is very close in meaning, but it focuses more specifically on being likable and friendly in social situations — it emphasizes how well someone gets along with others. Good-natured is broader and includes the idea of emotional steadiness and cheerfulness.

Affable means easy and pleasant to talk to. It highlights approachability. Good-natured includes that, but also the idea of not getting easily upset.

Genial means warm and cheerful in a sociable way — very similar to good-natured, but genial is often used in more formal or literary contexts.

Easygoing means relaxed and unbothered. It overlaps significantly with good-natured but focuses more on being laid-back and stress-free, while good-natured also carries warmth and kindness.

Pleasant simply means agreeable or enjoyable. It's more general and doesn't carry the deeper idea of a stable inner temperament.

Of all these, good-natured is the richest because it captures the whole package — kindness, cheerfulness, patience, and emotional warmth — all rooted in who a person naturally is at their core.

If you had to remember just one thing: a good-natured person is someone whose natural, default personality is warm, cheerful, patient, and easy to be around — and who stays that way without much effort, because that's simply who they are.
7101: "Goodly" means impressively large in size or amount, or in older usage, attractive and pleasing to look at. It always carries a sense of approval — like you're not just describing something, you're quietly admiring it.

Meaning 1: Large, Considerable, Substantial

(This is the meaning you'll encounter most often today)

When someone says "a goodly amount" or "a goodly number," they mean an amount or number that is notably large — large enough to be impressive or satisfying. Think of it as "large" with a warm nod of appreciation built into it.

This is the subtle but important difference: "large" is neutral. "Goodly" leans positive. It suggests the size is a good thing, even something to be pleased about.

Examples:

  • "A goodly number of volunteers showed up for the event."

(= A pleasingly large number — more than you might have expected, and that's a good thing.)

  • "She saved a goodly sum of money over the years."

(= A substantial, commendable amount.)

  • "We walked a goodly distance before we found shelter."

(= A considerable distance — enough to be noteworthy.)

  • "He had a goodly collection of rare books."

(= An impressively large collection.)

Notice that in all these cases, "goodly" is used right before a noun. This is almost always how it works. You say "a goodly portion", not "the portion is goodly."

Meaning 2: Attractive, Handsome, Pleasing to the Eye

(This is the older meaning — mostly found in literature, the Bible, and older texts)

In older English — the kind you find in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, or classic literature — "goodly" was used to describe something or someone that was beautiful, handsome, or pleasant to look at. It meant fine, impressive, and visually pleasing.

Examples from this older usage:

  • "He was a goodly young man — tall, strong, and fair."

(= Handsome and impressive in appearance.)

  • "They looked out upon a goodly land, full of green fields and clear rivers."

(= A beautiful, pleasing land.)

  • "It was a goodly ship, built with great skill."

(= A fine, impressive-looking ship.)

You are unlikely to use this meaning in everyday modern conversation, but you will come across it when reading older books, the Bible, or historical writing — so it's very useful to recognize it.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Goodly" is a formal and slightly old-fashioned word. Native speakers today rarely use it in casual conversation. You would not typically say "I ate a goodly pizza last night." But it appears regularly in:

  • Formal writing
  • Literature and historical texts
  • Speeches and essays that aim for a dignified, elevated tone
  • Phrases that are deliberately classical or literary in style

When a modern writer uses "goodly," they are often doing it deliberately to give their writing a sense of gravity, tradition, or quiet elegance.
The Key Feeling Behind the Word

No matter which meaning is being used, "goodly" always carries appreciation and approval. It is never cold or neutral. When something is described as "goodly," the speaker or writer is subtly saying: "This is good. This is worth noting. This is more than just ordinary."

This is what makes "goodly" more interesting than plain synonyms like "large" or "attractive." It packages a quiet compliment inside a simple descriptor.

Primary modern meaningLarge, considerable, substantial in amount or size — with a sense of approval
Older/literary meaningAttractive, handsome, pleasing to look at
ToneFormal, old-fashioned, warm, appreciative
How it's usedAlmost always directly before a noun: "a goodly sum," "a goodly man"
Where you'll see itBooks, literature, the Bible, formal or elevated writing

In a single sentence: "goodly" means impressively large (in modern use) or attractively fine-looking (in older use), and it always carries a tone of quiet admiration.
7102:
"Goodness knows" is an idiom used in two closely related ways:

First, it means that something is completely unknown, uncertain, or impossible to say with confidence. It signals that the speaker has no idea about something, or that the answer is a mystery.

Second, it is used to strongly emphasize a point — to stress that something is very true, very real, or has happened many times.

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand its roots.

The original phrase was "God knows." This is a very old expression that people used when they wanted to say, "Only God has the answer to this — humans don't." It suggested that something was beyond ordinary human knowledge.

However, in many cultures — especially in Christian traditions — using God's name casually in everyday conversation was considered disrespectful, even sinful. This is based on the biblical commandment: "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain."

So, over time, people started replacing the word "God" with softer, safer substitutes. The word "goodness" was one such substitute. This kind of polite replacement is called a minced oath — a watered-down version of a stronger expression that avoids causing offence.

So, "goodness knows" is simply a more polite, socially acceptable way of saying "God knows." Both mean the same thing. The only difference is that "goodness knows" avoids religious reference.

You can see this same pattern in other phrases too:

  • "Oh my God" became "Oh my goodness"
  • "For God's sake" became "For goodness' sake"
  • "God damn it" became "Gosh darn it"
The Two Main Uses, Explained Clearly

Use 1 — Expressing That Something Is Unknown

When someone says "goodness knows" before or after a statement, they are telling you: "I have absolutely no idea" or "Nobody can say for certain."

It adds a sense of mystery, confusion, or helplessness about knowing the answer.

Examples:

  • "Goodness knows where I left my keys."
    → The speaker has no clue where the keys are.
  • "Goodness knows how long this traffic will last."
    → It's impossible to predict how long the traffic will continue.
  • "He disappeared last night. Goodness knows what happened to him."
    → Nobody knows what happened to him.
  • "Goodness knows why she made that decision."
    → The reason is a complete mystery.

In all these cases, "goodness knows" is doing the job of saying: "It is beyond anyone's knowledge."

Use 2 — Emphasizing That Something Is Very True

Here, "goodness knows" is not about ignorance or mystery. Instead, it is used to add emotional weight and stress to a statement — to say: "This is absolutely, definitely true — believe me."

It often carries feelings of frustration, exhaustion, or strong conviction — especially when the speaker has been through a lot.

Examples:

  • "Goodness knows I've tried to help him."
    → I have certainly and repeatedly tried to help him. (Said with some frustration.)
  • "Goodness knows she deserves a holiday — she's been working non-stop."
    → She definitely and without any doubt deserves a holiday.
  • "Goodness knows, I told you this would happen!"
    → I am strongly emphasizing that I warned you about this.
  • "He's not a bad person. Goodness knows he has a kind heart."
    → It is absolutely true that he has a kind heart.

In this use, think of "goodness knows" as working like the words "certainly," "definitely," or "without a doubt" — but with more emotion and personality.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Being Used

The context of the sentence always tells you which meaning is intended.

  • If the sentence is about not knowing something, a mystery, or uncertainty → it's Use 1 (unknown).
  • If the sentence is about confirming, emphasizing, or stressing something → it's Use 2 (emphasis).

Sometimes, the two meanings can slightly overlap, giving the phrase a rich, layered feel. For example:

"Goodness knows I've been patient enough!"

This could mean both: "I have certainly been patient enough" (emphasis) AND there's a subtle hint that even the speaker is somewhat bewildered by how much patience they've shown.
The Tone and Feeling Behind the Phrase

"Goodness knows" is rarely a neutral expression. It almost always carries some emotional colour. Depending on the context, it can express:

  • Frustration → "Goodness knows I've told him a hundred times!"
  • Exasperation → "Goodness knows how we're going to fix this mess."
  • Wonder or admiration → "Goodness knows how she manages to stay so calm."
  • Sympathy → "Goodness knows she's had a difficult life."
  • Resignation → "Goodness knows what will happen next."

Since "goodness knows" originally replaced "God knows," there is a whole family of similar idioms that all share the same core meaning. All of them can be used in the same ways — to express the unknown or to emphasize:

  • "God knows" — the original, stronger version; less polite in formal or religious contexts
  • "Heaven knows" — another religious substitute, very common in British English
  • "Lord knows" — similarly polite and emphatic
  • "Who knows" — more casual; mainly used to express uncertainty
  • "Beats me" — very informal; only used to say "I have no idea"
  • "Your guess is as good as mine" — used only for the "unknown" meaning

Among all of these, "goodness knows," "heaven knows," and "Lord knows" are the closest in meaning and tone to each other. They are all polite, emotionally expressive, and suitable in both formal and informal speech.
Formality Level — Where and When to Use It

"Goodness knows" sits comfortably in everyday, informal to semi-formal English. It is perfectly fine to say in:

  • Casual conversations with friends or family
  • Workplace small talk
  • Personal writing, letters, or messages
  • Novels and storytelling (it makes characters sound natural and expressive)

It would feel slightly out of place in a strictly formal document (like a legal report or academic essay), where you would simply write "it is unknown" or "it is unclear."

It is used widely in both British and American English, though it has a slightly more old-fashioned, warm flavour that you'll notice more often in British speech and literature.
A Few More Examples to Cement Your Understanding

Expressing the unknown:

  • "Goodness knows what time he'll get home tonight."
  • "The project has been delayed again — goodness knows when it will actually be finished."
  • "She walked out without saying a word. Goodness knows what was going through her mind."

Adding emphasis:

  • "Goodness knows this job hasn't been easy, but we got through it."
  • "I'm not angry at him. Goodness knows he meant well."
  • "She's been through so much. Goodness knows she's a strong woman."
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you need to remember just one core idea about this idiom, let it be this:

"Goodness knows" = either "Nobody knows / It is a complete mystery" OR "It is absolutely, certainly true." Which meaning it carries depends entirely on the context — and the context always makes it clear.

It is a phrase full of feeling, rooted in history, and used every single day by fluent English speakers to make their language sound natural, warm, and expressive.
7103:
Goodwill means a sincere, warm, and positive feeling or attitude toward other people — a genuine desire to be kind, helpful, or friendly, without wanting anything in return. Think of it as the feeling in your heart when you truly wish someone well and are willing to act on it.

It is important to note that goodwill is always voluntary. Nobody forces you into it. It comes from a place of genuine generosity or friendliness, not obligation.
Meaning 1: Friendly or Benevolent Feeling Toward Others

This is the most everyday use of the word. When a person, a group, or even a nation holds a warm, cooperative, and friendly attitude toward another, that attitude is called goodwill.

Examples:

  • Two countries that were once enemies begin trading food and supplies with each other. This act signals that they no longer wish each other harm — it is a gesture of goodwill.
  • A neighbor brings you soup when you are sick, not because they owe you anything, but simply because they care. That kindness comes from goodwill.
  • After a long argument, two friends decide to let go of their anger and make peace. They approach each other with goodwill — a sincere desire to rebuild the relationship.

Notice that goodwill is not just politeness. Politeness can be fake. Goodwill is deeper — it is a real, positive intention toward the other person.
Meaning 2: Cheerful Willingness and a Cooperative Spirit

Goodwill can also describe the attitude with which someone does something. When a person takes on a task or agrees to something willingly, without resentment, and with a positive spirit, they do it with goodwill.

Examples:

  • An employee is asked to work late to help the team meet a deadline. Instead of complaining, she agrees cheerfully and puts in her best effort. She acts with goodwill.
  • A student accepts constructive criticism from a teacher, not defensively, but with an open mind and a cooperative attitude. That is goodwill.

In this sense, goodwill captures something close to goodhearted cooperation — doing something with a positive, generous spirit rather than reluctantly or resentfully.
Meaning 3: The Business and Accounting Meaning

This is a more specialized but very important meaning. In the world of business and finance, goodwill refers to the extra value a business has beyond what you can physically see or count.

To understand this, imagine you want to buy a small bakery. You count up everything the bakery owns: the oven, the tables, the ingredients in storage, the cash in the register. All of that adds up to, say, $100,000.

But you decide to pay $130,000 for the bakery instead.

Why would you pay $30,000 more than what the physical things are worth? Because the bakery has something invisible but extremely valuable: its reputation. It has a loyal group of regular customers who come every single morning. The bakery's name is trusted in the neighborhood. People love it. The previous owner spent years building those relationships and that reputation. You are buying that too.

That extra $30,000 you paid — the value of the reputation, the loyal customers, the trusted name — is called goodwill in business accounting. It gets recorded as an asset in the company's financial books, even though you cannot touch it or put it in a box.

Goodwill in business can come from many sources:

  • A strong, recognizable brand name (like a world-famous coffee chain)
  • A large base of loyal, repeat customers
  • A long-standing positive reputation in the market
  • Special knowledge, skills, or trade secrets the business has
  • Strong relationships with suppliers or partners

The key idea is this: a business that people trust and love is worth more than a business of the same size that nobody has heard of or cares about. The extra worth that comes from being trusted and loved — that is goodwill.

These meanings are not random — they all grow from the same root idea. In everyday life, goodwill is the positive, warm feeling one person holds toward another. When a business earns the trust, loyalty, and positive feeling of thousands of customers over many years, it has essentially built up a huge amount of goodwill in this original sense. People feel good about the business.

Accountants and businesspeople recognized that this collected positive feeling has real financial value — sometimes enormous value — and so they borrowed the word "goodwill" to name it. The business meaning is simply what happens when goodwill (the feeling) scales up to a company level and gets assigned a dollar amount.

A gesture of goodwill — An action done to show friendly or peaceful intentions, especially when trying to build or repair a relationship. "As a gesture of goodwill, the company offered a full refund without any questions."

A sign of goodwill — Similar to above; evidence that someone's intentions are positive. "Releasing the hostages was seen as a sign of goodwill before the peace talks began."

Out of goodwill — Doing something purely from kindness, with no expectation of reward. "She tutored the younger students out of goodwill."

Goodwill ambassador — A person (often famous) appointed to travel and represent a positive, friendly message on behalf of an organization or country.

Goodwill mission — A diplomatic trip or visit whose purpose is to build friendly relations between parties.

Goodwill sits somewhere between simple politeness and deep love. It is warmer than politeness (which can be hollow) but broader and less intense than love or deep friendship. It is the kind of feeling you might have toward a stranger you want to help, toward a neighbor you have always gotten along with, or toward a country you have no quarrel with. It is a baseline of warmth and positive intention — and that is precisely what makes it valuable, both between people and in business.
7104: The word goody has a few distinct meanings depending on context. Here is each one explained fully.
Meaning 1: A treat, gift, or anything pleasurable (the most common use)

This is by far the most widely used meaning today. A goody is something that is desirable, pleasing, or enjoyable — something that makes you happy to receive or experience. It is most often used in the plural form: goodies.

The word carries a warm, enthusiastic, slightly childlike energy. It suggests that whatever you are talking about is not just good, but delightfully good — something you'd get excited about.

It can refer to:

Food treats. This is the most classic use. Cookies, chocolates, sweets, candies — these are all goodies. If your grandmother baked you a batch of brownies and packed them in a tin, those are goodies.

"The kids rushed to the table full of goodies at the birthday party."
"She pulled a warm cookie from the oven — just one of the many goodies she'd prepared."

Small gifts, prizes, or freebies. When you attend an event, a conference, or a party and receive small surprise gifts or fun extras, those are goodies too. This led to the very common phrase "goody bag" — a small bag filled with little gifts or treats given to guests, usually at parties or promotional events.

"Everyone at the conference got a goody bag with a pen, a notebook, and some snacks."
"The children left the birthday party with goody bags."

Anything extra-special or exciting. More broadly, a goody can be any exciting bonus, perk, or feature — not just physical objects or food.

"The video game came with a lot of goodies for early buyers — bonus levels, special costumes, and a digital art book."
"Subscribe to the newsletter and receive exclusive goodies every month."
Meaning 2: A "good person" in a story (the hero, the protagonist)

In this meaning — used especially in British English and most common in the context of films, TV shows, books, and children's stories — a goody is a character who is on the good side. The goodies are the heroes, the protagonists, the people you are meant to root for.

The natural opposite of a goody in this context is a baddie (the villain).

"In old Western movies, the goodies wore white hats and the baddies wore black hats."
"My little brother always wants to play the goody. He refuses to be the villain."
"By the end of the film, all the goodies survived and the baddies were defeated."

This use is especially common when speaking to or about children, or when discussing entertainment in a playful, informal tone.
Meaning 3: An old, respected older woman (archaic — very old usage)

This is an archaic meaning, meaning it is very old and no longer used in everyday modern speech. You will mainly encounter it when reading old literature, historical texts, or stories set in past centuries (particularly 17th and 18th century England or early America).

In this meaning, Goody was a title of address — similar to how we say "Mrs." today. It was a shortened form used for a married woman of humble or lower social standing. You would use it with the woman's last name: Goody Brown, Goody Parker, and so on.

"Goody Osburn was called to the village meeting." (the kind of sentence you'd find in a historical novel)

It was not considered rude — it was simply the polite, everyday title for ordinary married women who were not of noble rank. Think of it as the common woman's equivalent of "Madam" or "Mistress."

Here is a quick mental picture of each meaning:

Goodies (treats/gifts): Imagine a child opening a party bag — chocolates, stickers, a little toy. Every single thing in that bag is a goody. The child's eyes light up. That feeling of delight and pleasure is exactly what the word carries.

Goody (hero in a story): Imagine a superhero in a cape fighting a villain. The superhero is the goody. Simple, clean moral categories — good vs. evil — and goody sits firmly on the good side.

Goody (old title): Imagine a historical village in the 1600s. A farmer's wife walks by. Someone greets her: "Good morning, Goody Miller." That's it — a respectful, ordinary title for an everyday woman of that era.

The word goody is informal. It belongs to casual, everyday speech — friendly conversation, marketing copy, children's language, and storytelling. You would not use it in a formal essay, a business letter, or an academic paper. In formal writing, you'd replace it with words like treats, rewards, gifts, perks, or protagonist depending on the meaning you want.
7105:
A goody-goody is a person who always behaves in an extremely well-mannered, rule-following, and morally "perfect" way — but does so in a way that feels fake, excessive, or done purely to impress others, especially people in authority (like teachers, parents, or bosses).

The key thing to understand is this: a goody-goody is not simply a good person. The word carries a negative, mocking tone. When you call someone a goody-goody, you are criticising them, not complimenting them.

A goody-goody typically shows one or more of these behaviours:

1. They follow every rule perfectly — but for the wrong reasons.
A genuinely good person follows rules because they believe it's the right thing to do. A goody-goody follows rules primarily to be seen as good, to earn praise, or to avoid any criticism whatsoever. Their goodness is performed for an audience.

2. They are excessively eager to please authority.
A goody-goody goes out of their way to impress teachers, managers, or parents — agreeing with everything they say, volunteering for tasks, and always being on their best behaviour when someone important is watching.

3. They report or expose other people's wrongdoings.
A classic goody-goody is quick to tell on others — "Teacher, he didn't do his homework!" — not necessarily because they care about fairness, but because it makes them look even better by comparison.

4. They are self-righteous.
They often have a subtle air of superiority, as if they are better than people who bend the rules, have fun in "wrong" ways, or aren't as "perfect" as they are. They may silently — or openly — judge others.

5. Their goodness feels hollow or exaggerated.
There's something about a goody-goody that feels insincere. Real virtue tends to be quiet. A goody-goody's virtue tends to be loud, visible, and convenient — it appears exactly when someone important might notice.

The word goody-goody is informal and gently contemptuous — somewhere between teasing and insulting. It's the kind of word peers use, not teachers or bosses. When someone calls you a goody-goody, they're saying:

"You're trying too hard to be perfect, and it's annoying. Relax. Stop performing. You're not as innocent as you pretend to be."

It also carries a slightly childish, mocking quality — the very sound of the word (repeating "goody" twice) mimics the way children taunt each other, which reinforces that the criticism is about someone being immature in their need for approval.
The Crucial Distinction: Goody-Goody vs. a Genuinely Good Person

This is the most important thing to understand about this word.

Genuinely Good PersonGoody-Goody
Why they behave wellBecause they truly believe in itTo gain approval or praise
How they treat othersWith genuine kindnessMay judge or look down on others
Are they consistent?Yes, even when no one is watchingMostly when someone important is watching
How others feel around themComfortable, respectedAnnoyed, judged

A saint is not a goody-goody. A monk is not a goody-goody. Your genuinely kind, humble neighbour is not a goody-goody. But the student who always reminds the teacher about homework, always sits perfectly straight when the principal walks in, and always makes sure everyone knows how well-behaved they are — that person is a goody-goody.

• "Don't be such a goody-goody — just skip one class with us."

(Friends pressuring someone to loosen up and stop being so rigidly rule-following.)

  • "Everyone in the office thinks he's a goody-goody because he praises every single idea the manager has."

(A colleague who is overly eager to please the boss.)

  • "She told the teacher we were whispering during the film. What a goody-goody."

(A classmate who reported others to look good herself.)

  • "I used to be a real goody-goody at school — never broke a single rule."

(Someone reflecting on their own past behaviour, slightly self-deprecatingly.)

The plural is goody-goodies.

"The class was full of goody-goodies who competed to answer every question first."
One Final Thought to Lock It In

Think of it this way: if goodness were a performance in a theatre, a goody-goody is the actor who never breaks character — not because they love the play, but because they desperately want a standing ovation. The audience (their peers) eventually finds it exhausting and a little dishonest. That exhaustion and mild contempt is exactly what the word "goody-goody" expresses.
7106:
"Goof off" means to waste time by avoiding your responsibilities — doing nothing useful, playing around, or acting silly when you are supposed to be working, studying, or doing something important.

Think of it this way: Imagine a student who sits at his desk with his books open, but instead of studying, he's doodling, staring at the ceiling, and throwing paper balls. He is goofing off. He's physically present, but mentally and productively — he's checked out.
Breaking Down the Word

To truly understand the idiom, it helps to understand the word "goof" first.

"Goof" (as a noun) means a silly, foolish, or irresponsible person — someone who doesn't take things seriously and acts childishly. Think of a class clown who never pays attention.

"Goof" (as a verb) means to act foolishly or make a careless mistake.

Now, when you add "off" to it, it becomes the phrasal verb "goof off," which means to be that goofy, unserious person — to avoid your duties and waste time being silly or idle when you should be doing something productive.

So "goof off" literally captures the idea of acting like a goof instead of doing what you're supposed to do.
Part of Speech

"Goof off" is a phrasal verb — a verb combined with a particle ("off") that creates a new, specific meaning together.

It conjugates like any regular verb:

  • Base form: goof off
  • Present: I/you/we/they goof off | He/she/it goofs off
  • Past tense: goofed off
  • Present participle (ongoing action): goofing off
Examples in Sentences

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how it naturally flows:

At school:

"Stop goofing off and pay attention to the teacher!"
"She goofed off the entire semester and failed her exams."

At work:

"The manager caught him goofing off on his phone instead of finishing the report."
"We all goof off a little on Friday afternoons."

At home:

"Instead of cleaning the house, he spent the whole day goofing off and watching TV."

In a light/friendly tone:

"Let's goof off this afternoon — we deserve a break."
"We goofed off all summer as kids. It was wonderful."
Tone and Register — When and Where to Use It

"Goof off" is informal and colloquial. This means:

  • ✅ Use it in casual everyday conversations with friends, family, or colleagues you're friendly with.
  • ✅ Use it when writing informal messages or texts.
  • ❌ Do not use it in formal writing like business emails, academic essays, or professional reports.

Instead of "He goofed off during the meeting," you would write formally: "He was inattentive and unproductive during the meeting."

It is most common in American English. Speakers of British English will generally understand it, but they are less likely to use this specific phrase themselves.
The Tone of the Phrase — Is It Harsh or Light?

"Goof off" carries a somewhat playful or light tone, even when used as a criticism. It suggests someone is being childish or silly about avoiding work — not cruel or malicious.

Compare these:

  • "He shirked his duties" — sounds very serious and formal, suggests a serious failure of responsibility.
  • "He goofed off" — sounds more casual, slightly humorous, more like a scolding you'd give a child or a friend.

However, don't be fooled by the playful sound — when a boss or teacher says "Stop goofing off!" it is absolutely a reprimand and should be taken seriously.
The Noun Form — "A Goof-off"

You can also use it as a noun to describe a person who habitually wastes time and avoids work:

"Don't be such a goof-off!"
"He's the biggest goof-off in the office — he never meets his deadlines."

Notice the hyphen when used as a noun: goof-off.
Similar Expressions (and How They Differ)

Understanding related phrases will sharpen your understanding:

1. Slack off — Similar to "goof off" but slightly more serious in tone. It emphasizes a consistent pattern of doing less than expected, often out of laziness.

"He's been slacking off at work for months."

2. Fool around — Very similar to "goof off"; means to waste time doing silly or purposeless things. Can also mean to joke and not be serious.

"Stop fooling around and get to work."

3. Mess around — Also means to spend time without a clear purpose or to tinker aimlessly.

"We just messed around at the park all day."

4. Laze around / Loaf around — To relax and do nothing, usually without the "silly" connotation. It's more about pure idleness than silliness.

"I lazed around the house all weekend."

Key difference: "Goof off" specifically suggests a childlike, unserious, or playful avoidance of responsibility. The others can feel more neutral or lazy without the "silly" flavour.
Related but Different — "Goof Up"

Don't confuse "goof off" with "goof up." They are related in family but completely different in meaning:

  • Goof off = waste time, avoid responsibilities
  • Goof up = make a careless mistake

"I goofed up the recipe and put in too much salt." (I made a mistake)
"I goofed off instead of cooking dinner." (I avoided the task)
Etymology — Where Did It Come From?

The word "goof" entered American slang in the early 20th century (around the 1910s–1920s). It likely descended from an old English dialect word "goff," meaning a foolish or stupid person, which itself may have roots in the old French word "goffe," meaning awkward or clumsy.

The phrasal verb "goof off" developed in American English in the mid-20th century (1930s–1950s), growing out of military and everyday slang to describe soldiers or workers who avoided their duties in a lazy, silly way.
Quick Summary

MeaningTo waste time; avoid work or responsibilities in a silly, lazy, or playful way
TypePhrasal verb (also a noun: "a goof-off")
RegisterInformal, casual
OriginAmerican English, mid-20th century
TonePlayful but still a criticism

The next time someone tells you to "stop goofing off," you'll know exactly what they mean — and now you know far more about this little phrase than most native speakers ever stop to think about.
7107: A goofball is a person who is silly, playful, and a little foolish — someone who acts in a goofy, clownish, or absurd way, often just to get a laugh or simply because that is their natural personality. Think of someone who makes ridiculous faces, tells dumb jokes that make no sense, trips over their own feet, or does something hilariously pointless just to entertain others. That person is a goofball.

This is crucial to understand: goofball is almost always a warm, affectionate word. It is not a serious insult. When someone calls you a goofball, they are usually smiling while they say it. It carries a sense of fondness — the kind of teasing you do with someone you like. It is very different from calling someone stupid or an idiot, which are harsh and mean. Calling someone a goofball says, "You're being silly, and honestly, I find it kind of charming."

To fully picture a goofball, here are the kinds of behaviors the word describes:

  • Making silly voices or funny faces for no serious reason
  • Doing something ridiculous and laughing at themselves
  • Playing childish pranks that are harmless and goofy
  • Being clumsy or awkward in an amusing way
  • Saying something so nonsensical that everyone just laughs and shakes their head
  • Dancing badly and proudly in public
  • Not taking themselves — or life — too seriously

The key idea is that a goofball's silliness is lighthearted, harmless, and usually good-natured. They are not dangerous, not mean, just... entertainingly foolish.
Who (or What) Can Be Called a Goofball?

While it most naturally describes a person, it can also be used for:

  • Children — very commonly. Kids who act silly are the classic image of a goofball.
  • Adults — an adult who hasn't lost their playful, childlike humor.
  • Pets — especially dogs. "My dog ran into the glass door and then wagged his tail. Total goofball." This usage is very natural and common.
  • Fictional characters — a clumsy, funny character in a movie or cartoon is often described as a goofball.

• "He wore a banana costume to the grocery store just to make his kids laugh. What a goofball."
  • "She's such a goofball — she spent ten minutes telling a joke and then forgot the punchline."
  • "I love my cat. She chases her own tail every morning. Absolute goofball."
  • "Come on, stop being a goofball and pay attention for five minutes!" (said with a smile, not real anger)
  • "Even at fifty, my dad is the biggest goofball in the room — always the first one making silly voices."

There is a second, much older meaning of goofball that you may occasionally come across in old books, old films, or old American music — particularly from the 1940s to 1960s. In that era, goofball was street slang for a barbiturate pill — a type of strong sedative or sleeping pill that was widely misused. This usage has largely disappeared from everyday modern conversation, but it is worth knowing so you are not confused if you encounter it in an older context.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what this word does not mean:

  • It does not mean someone is deeply stupid or lacks intelligence. A goofball can be very smart — they're just choosing to be silly.
  • It does not carry real anger or contempt. If someone is genuinely furious with you, they would not call you a goofball.
  • It is not a formal word. You would not use it in a professional report, an academic essay, or a serious conversation. It belongs entirely in casual, everyday speech.

If you had to boil goofball down to its absolute essence: it is a person whose defining quality is harmless, playful silliness. The word is soft, warm, and a little bit fond. It is the kind of label that is given not with a frown, but almost always with a laugh.
7108:
"Goofy" means silly, playful, or mildly ridiculous in a completely harmless, lighthearted way. When something or someone is goofy, they make you smile or chuckle — not because they're clever or witty, but because they're being innocently, freely, unashamedly silly.

Think of a dog frantically chasing its own tail. Think of a friend who makes a ridiculous face just to make you laugh. Think of someone tripping over nothing and then bursting into laughter at themselves. That gentle, warm, silly energy is exactly what "goofy" captures.
The most important thing: its emotional tone

This is what separates "goofy" from similar words and what you must feel in your bones to truly understand it. Goofy is almost always a warm, affectionate word. It is not an insult. When you call someone goofy, you are not cutting them down — you are looking at them fondly, perhaps teasing them a little, and finding their silliness lovable.

Compare these two sentences: "You're stupid" lands like a punch. "You're goofy" lands like a laugh and a nudge on the shoulder. One stings; the other smiles. A parent watching their child make ridiculous faces at the dinner table might say, "Oh, you're so goofy!" — and it's pure affection. That warmth is baked into the word itself.
What can be described as goofy?

Almost anything. A person can have a goofy personality, meaning they are naturally silly, playful, and don't take themselves too seriously. A smile can be goofy — this is actually one of the most common uses. A "goofy grin" is a wide, uncontrolled, slightly silly-looking smile, the kind that spreads across your face when you're really happy or being playful and you can't hold it back. An idea can be goofy, meaning it sounds silly or a little nonsensical, though even then the word says so gently rather than harshly. A movie can be goofy, meaning it is light, silly, and deliberately doesn't take itself seriously. An outfit, a joke, a dance move, a laugh — all of these can be goofy.

Here are some examples across these uses:

"He has such a goofy sense of humor — he does silly voices and laughs at his own jokes."
"She walked in with a goofy grin on her face and we knew something good had happened."
"It's a goofy little film, but it's fun."
"That hat looks a bit goofy, but honestly it suits you."
"The kids were being completely goofy at the table, giggling at everything."
"Stop being so goofy and help me with this!"

Notice that last one — even used as a mild scolding, it still sounds warm and playful, not genuinely angry.
How goofy compares to similar words

Silly is the closest word to goofy and the two are often interchangeable. However, "goofy" tends to feel slightly more specific and more personal — it suggests a distinct, endearing quality of unself-conscious silliness, almost like a personality trait rather than just a momentary behavior.

Dorky is also similar, but it carries a stronger undertone of social awkwardness. A dorky person might seem a little embarrassed or unaware of how they come across. A goofy person, by contrast, is often completely at ease — they're not awkward so much as freely, happily silly.

Wacky and zany suggest something more extreme, eccentric, or over-the-top. Goofy is gentler and far more everyday.

Ridiculous can overlap with goofy, but "ridiculous" is stronger and can carry a negative or frustrated edge. Goofy never really does.

Funny is broader — something can be funny because it's clever, dark, surprising, or satirical. Goofy is specifically the innocent, lighthearted, silly variety of funny.

Goofy scales naturally. Something can be a little goofy (just mildly silly), pretty goofy (noticeably silly in a fun way), or absolutely goofy (so silly it's almost absurd, but still harmless and warm). You can also say someone "acts goofy" when they're in a particularly silly mood, even if they aren't always like that.
Register: when and where to use it

Goofy is a casual, informal word. It fits perfectly in everyday conversation, with friends and family, in relaxed writing, and in descriptions of entertainment or pop culture. It would feel out of place in formal or professional writing. You might say "that was a goofy idea" to a friend, but you wouldn't write it in a business email or academic paper. In informal contexts, though, it is a very natural, widely used, and well-understood word.

To put it all together: "goofy" describes a kind of silliness that is innocent, harmless, and often lovable. It carries no cruelty, no serious criticism, and no edge. It is the silliness of a child making faces, of a friend doing a ridiculous impression, of a comedy that revels in its own absurdity. When you call something or someone goofy, you are almost always smiling when you say it — and that smile is part of the word's meaning.
7109: "Goon" is an informal, slang word. It has two main meanings that are quite different from each other, so understanding both is important.
Meaning 1: A stupid or foolish person

In this sense, a goon is someone who acts in a silly, dim-witted, or clumsy way — someone who lacks common sense or does something embarrassingly dumb.

This usage is usually light-hearted and not deeply insulting. Friends often call each other goons in a playful, teasing way. If your friend trips over nothing and falls flat on their face, you might laugh and say, "You absolute goon!"

Think of it as a softer, funnier version of calling someone a fool, a dunce, or an idiot — but without the real sting of those words. The tone is more amused than angry.
Meaning 2: A hired thug or violent enforcer

This is the more serious and more widely used meaning in modern English. Here, a goon is a large, intimidating person — usually hired or employed — whose job is to threaten, intimidate, or physically harm others on someone else's behalf.

Picture a crime boss who has a few big, scary men following him around to do his dirty work. Those men are his goons. They don't need to be clever; they need to be threatening. A goon in this sense is essentially a muscle-for-hire: someone paid to rough people up, guard a place through fear, or act as an enforcer.

This meaning carries a strongly negative, menacing tone. The word signals that the person is not just violent but also mindlessly obedient — doing whatever their boss tells them without question or conscience. They're not seen as smart, sophisticated criminals; they're the blunt instruments of more powerful people.

You'll often see this in crime dramas, mob stories, and political thrillers. For example: "The gangster sent his goons to collect the debt."

A related phrase worth knowing is "goon squad" — a group of goons working together. A goon squad might be hired by a corrupt politician, a criminal organization, or a business to intimidate enemies, break up protests, or carry out violence. The phrase always suggests organized, deliberate intimidation by a group of people.

In ice hockey, a goon has a specific meaning: a player whose main role on the team is to fight and physically intimidate players on the opposing team, rather than to score goals or display skill. These players are sometimes also called "enforcers." Calling someone a goon in this context is not always an insult — it's just an honest description of their role, though it does suggest they rely on toughness and aggression more than talent.

In Australian slang, "goon" refers specifically to cheap wine that comes in a large cardboard box with a foil bag inside. This meaning is entirely regional and you'd only hear it used this way in Australia. If an Australian says, "We bought three goons for the party," they mean they bought several large boxes of inexpensive wine. This meaning has nothing to do with stupidity or violence — it's purely informal slang for a type of product.
How to tell which meaning is being used

Context makes it clear almost every time:

  • If someone is being called clumsy or foolish in a casual, light-hearted way → Meaning 1 (silly person)
  • If there's a threatening, criminal, or mob-like context → Meaning 2 (hired thug)
  • If the topic is ice hockey → Meaning 3 (enforcer)
  • If the speaker is Australian and talking about a party or drinking → Meaning 4 (boxed wine)

All four meanings are informal. You would not use "goon" in formal writing, academic work, or professional settings. It belongs to casual conversation, fiction, journalism covering crime or sports, and everyday speech.

The word is most at home in English-speaking countries like the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, though its specific meanings can vary slightly by country as shown above.
